title: Minimum Deletions to Make Array Beautiful
statement:
Call an array **beautiful** when its length is even and, for every even index `i`, the elements `nums[i]` and `nums[i + 1]` differ. In other words, splitting it into consecutive pairs (indices 0-1, 2-3, ...) gives pairs of two different values. The empty array counts as beautiful.

You may delete any elements of the integer array `nums`; the remaining elements close the gaps and keep their relative order. Return the smallest number of deletions that leaves a beautiful array.
notes:
## Intuition

Build the beautiful array from left to right. The kept elements fall into pairs; whenever a pair has only its first element so far, the next element must differ from it. If the next value equals that first element, one of the two has to go, and deleting the newcomer is never worse: both choices leave the same open pair start (same value) and the same remaining suffix. Otherwise keep it. At the end an unfinished pair (odd length) costs one more deletion. A brute force tries every subsequence; the greedy makes one pass.

## Approach

1. Keep a count `kept` of elements kept so far and `last`, the most recently kept value.
2. For each `value`: if `kept` is odd, the last kept element is waiting for a partner. If `value === last`, delete `value` (skip it).
3. Otherwise keep `value`: record it in `last` and increase `kept`.
4. If `kept` ends odd, delete the final kept element too.
5. The answer is `nums.length - kept`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 1, 2, 3, 5]`. Keep `1` (`kept = 1`). The next `1` would pair with an equal value, so it is deleted. Keep `2` (`kept = 2`, pair `1,2`), keep `3` (`kept = 3`), keep `5` (`kept = 4`, pair `3,5`). `kept` is even, so the answer is `5 - 4 = 1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- The pair rule is about positions **after** deletions; comparing `nums[i]` with `nums[i + 1]` at original even indices gives wrong answers once something has been deleted.
- Do not forget the final odd-length fix: `[1, 2, 3]` needs one deletion.
- Equal values are fine across pairs: `[1, 2, 2, 3]` is beautiful.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `kept` | number of elements kept so far |
| `last` | the most recently kept value |
| `value` | the element being considered |

narration.3: The most recently kept value; -1 never matches a real value.
narration.5: Decide each element in order, keep or delete.
narration.6: An odd count means the last kept element starts a pair; an equal value cannot complete it.
narration.7: Delete this element; the open pair keeps waiting for a different value.
narration.9: Keep the element: it either starts a new pair or completes the open one.
narration.12: An odd number of kept elements leaves a pair unfinished.
narration.13: Delete that last unpaired element as well.
narration.15: Every element not kept was deleted.
